opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest thing is having good taste about where the leverage is. A lot of people pick problems because they're intellectually interesting or because there's a nice clean benchmark to climb, and that's not necessarily where the marginal hour of effort buys you the most capability.

The way I think about it is: what is actually bottlenecking the model right now? If you sit down and look at transcripts of where it fails, really stare at them, you start to get a sense that it's not some exotic thing. It's that the model loses track over a long horizon, or it can't verify its own work, or it doesn't have the right feedback signal in some domain. Those are the problems worth working on, because if you crack them, everything downstream gets better.

The second thing is to bias heavily toward things that scale. There's this recurring lesson in the field where clever, hand-engineered tricks give you a nice bump and then get washed out by the next order of magnitude of compute. So when I'm evaluating an idea I ask, does this get better as we throw more compute at it, or does it get absorbed? If it's the latter, it's probably not worth a lot of your time unless it's unblocking something right now.

And third, I'd say pick problems where you can iterate fast. Research speed is so dominated by how quickly you can get signal. If your experiment takes three weeks to tell you anything, you'll get maybe fifteen shots a year. If you can find a smaller proxy that actually correlates with the big-scale behavior, you get hundreds of shots. A lot of the skill is in building that tight loop and being honest about whether your proxy is telling you the truth.

Then there's a bit of personal fit. You want to work on something where you have some unfair advantage, whether it's engineering skill, a particular intuition, or just being willing to do the unglamorous infrastructure work nobody else wants to do. Honestly, that last one is underrated. Some of the most impactful work I've seen came from people who just made the tooling ten times better, and suddenly everyone around them could move faster.

r001.rationale: The candidate recommends finding current model bottlenecks by studying failure transcripts, but does not clearly say to work backward from concrete problems one wants to solve.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses choosing ideas that scale with compute, but does not state that issues encountered while scaling models guide the next round of improvements.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that most of the value comes from a pretty mundane place, which is: look at where the model is actually failing, and ask why. There's this temptation, especially coming from academia, to pick the problem that feels intellectually clean or that would make a good paper. And I think that's often the wrong filter. The right filter is something like, what is the biggest gap between what the model does today and what we'd want it to do, and is that gap something I can actually measure and move?

So concretely, I'd say three things. First, pick problems where you can get a tight feedback loop. If it takes you three weeks to find out whether your idea worked, you're going to run maybe ten experiments a year, and you're going to be wrong about most of them. If you can get it down to hours, you learn so much faster, and honestly the quality of your intuitions compounds. A lot of the best researchers I've worked with are not necessarily the ones with the best initial ideas, they're the ones who have run the most experiments and gotten the most calibrated about what tends to work.

Second, I think you want to be a bit suspicious of problems that everyone agrees are important, because those tend to be crowded, and the marginal value of one more person is low. The really valuable stuff is often where you've noticed something slightly off in the data or the evals or the training dynamics that other people have walked past. That requires actually looking at the outputs. Like, reading them. Not just looking at the loss curve. I think people underrate how much you learn from staring at a few hundred model samples and going, huh, it keeps doing this weird thing.

And third, I'd think about scale. Will this still matter at ten times the compute? A lot of clever tricks are really just compensating for a lack of scale, and they wash out. The things that persist tend to be about the fundamental structure of the problem: how you get the right data, how you make the learning signal cleaner, how you let the model use more compute at inference time. If you can convince yourself your idea is in that category, that's a good sign.

But I'd also say, don't over-plan it. The field moves fast enough that a lot of problem selection is just being in the right place, paying attention, and being willing to drop what you're doing when something more important shows up.

r001.rationale: It recommends starting from where the model fails and identifying the biggest gap between current behavior and the desired behavior, then choosing a measurable gap to address.

r002.rationale: It asks whether a proposed idea will still matter at ten times the compute, but does not say that issues encountered while scaling models should guide the next round of improvements.

astra-6.text:
I think you want to start with a concrete picture of what the model ought to be able to do that it currently can’t. Where does it fail in a way that surprises you? And then ask whether that failure points to something more general. Is it missing knowledge, is it failing to learn from feedback, or does it know how to do each step but struggle to put them together?

The other thing I’d look for is a fast feedback loop. Can you run an experiment that would actually change your mind? You can have a very ambitious goal, but you want the next experiment to distinguish between explanations, rather than just give you a slightly better number.

And I think there’s a lot of value in spending time with the models. If you only look at aggregate benchmarks, you can miss both how capable they are and how strange their limitations are. Those observations are often a good starting point for choosing what to work on.

r001.rationale: It recommends starting from a concrete capability the model lacks and using that failure to choose what to work on.

r002.rationale: It says model failures and limitations can guide research choices, but does not connect issues encountered when scaling models to the next round of improvements.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you want to start with a concrete failure of the model that you can actually study. Where does it struggle on something that seems like it should be learnable? And can you make the experimental loop short enough that you’ll find out whether your explanation is right?

There’s a balance here. If you just chase whatever moves a benchmark, you can end up making improvements that don’t generalize. But if your question is “How do we get intelligence?” it’s very hard to get useful feedback. Ideally, you have a fairly ambitious hypothesis and a small experiment that could tell you you’re wrong.

I’d also ask whether the problem will still matter when the models get substantially better. Some weaknesses disappear with scale. Others become more important because they’re preventing you from using all the capability that’s already there. Finding those bottlenecks seems especially valuable.

r001.rationale: It recommends starting from a concrete model failure to study, but does not say to work backward from a concrete problem one wants to solve.

r002.rationale: It notes that some weaknesses change as models scale, but does not state that issues encountered during scaling should guide the next round of improvements.
